## 1. What you'll build, and why

Every program so far has computed with *fixed-shape* data: an `Int`, a `struct` with a known set
of fields, an `enum` with a known set of cases. Real programs need **collections** — a list whose
length isn't known until runtime — and **strings**. This concept builds the two foundational ones,
`Array<Int>` and `String`, **in our own subset**, on the **heap**, and confronts the question that
makes Swift's collections interesting: an array is *backed by a heap buffer* (a reference), yet it
*behaves like a value* (`var b = a` gives `b` its own logical copy). How? **Copy-on-write.**

This is also the first time the runtime library matters. Like concept 30's error register, the
whole feature lowers to **runtime intrinsics** (`rt.array_new`, `rt.array_push`, `rt.str_concat`,
…) — ordinary `apply`s of named runtime functions — so we add `Array` and `String` **without a
single new SIL instruction**. The compiler emits calls; a small hand-written LLVM runtime (given)
implements the buffer.

- **You implement:** the **copy-on-write dance** for the two mutators — `a.append(x)` and
  `a[i] = e` — the load / `make_unique` / store-back / mutate sequence that is the beating heart of
  Swift value semantics.
- **Outcome:** array and string programs — literals, `count`, subscript read/write, `append`,
  `for`-`in`, `+`, the out-of-bounds trap — matching `swiftc` byte-for-byte, with **`var b = a`
  then mutating `b` leaving `a` untouched**.

> **New to Swift?** In Swift, `Array`, `String`, `Dictionary`, every `struct`, and every `enum`
> are **value types**: assignment and parameter-passing behave as if they *copy*. Classes (concept
> 25) are the only **reference types**. So `var b = a; b.append(4)` must not change `a` — even
> though copying a million-element array on every assignment would be absurd. Copy-on-write is how
> Swift gets value *semantics* at reference *speed*.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### The buffer: a reference type wearing a value type's clothes

An `Array<Int>` value is a **pointer** to a heap **buffer**. Our buffer is a 32-byte header
followed (indirectly) by the elements:

```
buffer:  { i64 refcount; i64 count; i64 capacity; ptr data }
                  |            |          |          |
            how many      logical    allocated    -> [ e0, e1, …, e(cap-1) ]   (i64 × capacity)
            arrays share   length     slots
```

`count` is how many elements you've stored; `capacity` is how many the `data` block can hold
before it must grow. `append` past capacity **doubles** it (`max(4, 2·cap)`), `malloc`s a bigger
`data`, copies the old elements, and frees the old block — *amortized O(1)* push, the classic
growable-array trick. `data` is a *separate* allocation from the header so the header pointer
(the array value) stays stable across regrows.

A value of type `[Int]` is just that header pointer — 8 bytes, cheap to copy. Which is exactly the
problem: if `var b = a` copies the *pointer*, then `b` and `a` share one buffer, and `b.append(4)`
would be visible through `a`. That's reference semantics — wrong for a Swift value type.

### Copy-on-write: share until the first write

The fix is the **`refcount`** field and three operations:

- **retain** — *"another binding now shares this buffer."* `var b = a` bumps `refcount` (1 → 2).
  Both `a` and `b` point at the same buffer. No copy yet — reads are safe to share.
- **make_unique** — *the copy-on-write check.* Before any **mutation**, ask: is this buffer
  shared (`refcount > 1`)? If **no**, it's already mine — mutate in place. If **yes**, *make a
  fresh private copy* (and drop my share of the original, `refcount` → 1), then mutate the copy.
- the mutation itself (**push** / **set**) then runs on a buffer it is guaranteed to own alone.

![Copy-on-write: `var b = a` shares the buffer (refcount 2); `b.append(4)` sees refcount > 1, copies the buffer, and mutates the copy — so `a` still reads `[1,2,3]`. Value semantics from a reference, paid for by one refcount check per mutation.](figs/cow.png)

The figure is the whole idea. The cost of value semantics drops from *"copy on every assignment"*
to *"copy on the first mutation of a shared buffer"* — and a buffer that's never mutated while
shared (the overwhelmingly common case: pass an array to a function that only reads it) is **never
copied at all**. One `refcount` load + compare per mutation buys you safe, cheap sharing.

### How swiftc does exactly this

This is not a toy model — it is *literally* how Swift's `Array` works. Open
`stdlib/public/core/ContiguousArrayBuffer.swift`: every mutating method begins with a call to
**`isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&buffer)`** (or `_makeUniqueAndReserveCapacityIfNotUnique`), and
copies the storage only when it returns `false`. The storage object is a real Swift class with a
real ARC refcount — the same `refcount` word, the same retain on copy, the same
"unique-or-copy" check before a write. Our `rt.array_make_unique` *is*
`isKnownUniquelyReferenced` + the copy, fused. We use a hand-written i64 buffer where swiftc uses a
managed class; the *discipline* is identical.

> Oracle: `Array.swift` (the public API), `ContiguousArrayBuffer.swift` /
> `_ContiguousArrayBuffer` (the CoW storage + `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`), and
> `Builtin.isUnique` (the compiler intrinsic behind the check). Read a mutating method like
> `append` top-to-bottom — the uniqueness check is the first thing it does.

### The mutator's lowering — load, make_unique, store **back**, mutate

In SILGen, `a.append(x)` and `a[i] = e` both lower to the same four-step dance on the variable's
slot (`a`'s `alloc_stack`, which holds the buffer pointer):

```
%p   = load %slot                          ; the current buffer pointer
%uq  = apply @rt.array_make_unique(%p)     ; copies iff shared; returns a uniquely-owned pointer
store %uq to %slot                         ; <-- CRUCIAL: write the (maybe new) pointer back
%_   = apply @rt.array_push(%uq, %x)       ; mutate the buffer we now own alone
```

The **store-back** (step 3) is the step learners forget — and it's the subtle bug: if
`make_unique` copied, but you keep mutating through the *old* `%p` (or never write `%uq` back into
the slot), then `a` silently points at the un-mutated original and your write vanishes. Writing the
fresh pointer back into the slot is what makes the variable adopt its private copy. (`a[i] = e` is
identical, ending in `rt.array_set(%uq, %i, %x)`.)

By contrast, a **read** (`a[i]`, `a.count`, `for x in a`) never mutates, so it needs no
`make_unique` — it just `load`s the pointer and calls `rt.array_get` / `rt.array_count`. And
**construction** (`[1,2,3]`) makes a fresh buffer (`rt.array_new` + a `push` per element) that is
born uniquely owned (`refcount` 1), so it needs no retain. Only an **alias** (`var b = a`, where
the right-hand side is an existing array variable) retains.

### Bounds checking and the trap

`rt.array_get`/`rt.array_set` compare the index against `count`; out of range, they write
`Fatal error: Index out of range` to stderr and execute `llvm.trap` — **SIGTRAP, exit 133**, the
same crash (and message) `swiftc` produces. This reuses the trap mechanism from concept 13's
force-unwrap; an array access is a *checked* operation, and the check is part of the language's
memory-safety guarantee, not optional.

### String — a C-string, for now

`String` we keep deliberately simple: a value of type `String` is a `ptr` to a NUL-terminated
byte buffer (a literal is a private global; `s + t` `malloc`s `strlen(s)+strlen(t)+1` bytes and
copies both halves via `rt.str_concat`; `.count` is `strlen`; `print` is `printf("%s")`). For
ASCII this matches `swiftc` exactly. Swift's real `String` is far richer — UTF-8 storage,
small-string inlining, grapheme-cluster `count` — so for non-ASCII our byte `count` diverges from
swiftc's grapheme `count`. That's the documented boundary; concept 32 and beyond could close it.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Two punctuation tokens, added to `token.ml` and to `lexer.ml`'s punctuation
table — they were simply missing before this concept:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `[` | `Token.LBracket` | opens an array literal, a subscript, and the `[T]` type sugar |
| `]` | `Token.RBracket` | closes them |

`tokenize` also tracks the bracket DEPTH and drops `Newline` while it is above zero. A newline
inside brackets separates nothing — there is no statement there to separate — and swiftc reads
it that way too. Without it, `let a = [\n 1,\n 2\n]` was a parse error, and the stress corpus
had to write its boards on one line.

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05-30.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal. (The metasymbol `[ … ]` and the
Swift terminal `"[" … "]"` unavoidably share a shape here; the quotes tell them apart.)

```
type        ::= [ "any" ] ident [ "?" ]
              | "(" [ type { "," type } ] ")" "->" type
              | "[" type "]"                                        <-- new
                (v0 resolves only "[Int]"; see the diagnostics below)

primary     ::= …
              | "[" [ expr { "," expr } ] "]"                       <-- new
                (an array literal; empty needs an annotation to name
                 its element type)

postfix     ::= primary { "." ident [ "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")" ]
                        | "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")"
                        | "[" expr "]"                              <-- new  (subscript)
                        | "!" | ("as?" | "as!") ident }

statement   ::= …
              | postfix "[" expr "]" "=" expr                       <-- new  (subscript write)
              | "for" ident "in" expr block                         <-- new form: the operand
                                                                         may now be an ARRAY,
                                                                         not only a range
```

Three members and one operator come with the types rather than with the grammar, since they
are ordinary member syntax: `a.count`, `a.isEmpty` and `a.append(x)` on an array, `s.count` on
a String, and `+` on two Strings. None of them is a declared method anywhere — sema special-
cases the names on a `TArray`/`TString` receiver and SILGen turns each into one call into the
runtime.

### The diagnostics you emit

Neither hole produces a diagnostic — they are lowerings. All of these are given, and
`sema-arrays.t` keeps them on record. Three of them are places our subset is deliberately
smaller than Swift's, and each one says so rather than failing later and less clearly.

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `let names = ["a", "b"]` | `arrays of 'String' are not supported in this subset (only '[Int]'; element-generic buffers are this concept's exercise)` | **swiftc accepts.** The buffer is a homogeneous store of machine words; making it element-generic is exercise 1, and it is what unlocks concept 32 for other element types |
| `let a: [Int] = [1, "x"]` | `cannot convert value of type 'String' to specified type 'Int'` | `… to expected argument type 'Int'` — same refusal, swiftc names the site |
| `let a = [1, 2]` then `a.append(3)` | `cannot use mutating member on immutable value: 'a' is a 'let' constant` | **same**, character for character. Until this was checked, appending to a `let` array compiled and grew it |
| `let a = [1, 2]` then `a[0] = 5` | `cannot assign through subscript: 'a' is a 'let' constant` | **same** |
| `a[0][1]` | `value of type 'Int' has no subscripts` | **same** |
| `s[0]` on a String | `value of type 'String' has no subscripts` | swiftc: `'subscript(_:)' is unavailable: cannot subscript String with an Int, use a String.Index instead.` Both refuse; Swift's message points at `String.Index`, which we do not have |
| `for x in 5 { … }` | `type 'Int' is not a sequence` | **same** |
| `a.nope` | `value of type '[Int]' has no member 'nope'` | **same** |
| `print(a)` for an array | `cannot print a value of type '[Int]' (only Int, Double, Bool and String)` | **swiftc accepts** and prints `[1, 2]`. Printing an aggregate needs reflection |
| `a == b` for two arrays | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two '[Int]' operands` | **swiftc accepts** — `Array` is `Equatable` when its element is. Ours has no aggregate compare, and reaching IRGen this emitted an `add i64` on two pointers that clang refused |

One divergence has no diagnostic at all, because it is not an error: `s.count` counts **bytes**,
where Swift counts extended grapheme clusters. On ASCII they agree, which is why the corpus is
ASCII; on `"é"` or an emoji they do not, and a real `String` is exercise 5.

### The v0 scope, honestly

Our buffer is a homogeneous **`i64`** store, so v0 supports **`[Int]`** only. `[String]` or
`[Bool]` would need the buffer to hold pointers / i1s — an element-generic buffer with a
zext/ptr-cast at the boundary (exercise 1). Rather than miscompile them, sema **rejects**
non-`Int` element types with a clear message. Likewise, full ARC release of a buffer on scope exit
is elided (we leak — observably harmless, since stdout is unaffected); wiring arrays into concept
26's scope-release machinery is exercise 4.

## 3. Build it, step by step

You implement the two **copy-on-write mutators** in `silgen.ml`. Everything else — the `[T]`
parser and typing, literals, subscript *reads*, `count`/`isEmpty`, `for`-`in`, String, the
retain on `var b = a`, and the entire `rt.*` runtime in `irgen.ml` — is given.

1. **`TODO(31a)` — `a.append(x)`**, in the `Method_call` arm guarded by `is_array_recv`. You are
   handed `slot` (the array variable's `alloc_stack`), `elt` (the element type) and `xv` (the
   lowered argument); the four steps are the ones §2 spells out, and the third one is the one
   that is easy to leave out. The result of the whole arm is the `rt.array_push` call, typed
   `TVoid`.
2. **`TODO(31b)` — `a[i] = e`**, the `Set_subscript` statement. The same four steps, with `iv`
   and `xv` given, ending in `rt.array_set` rather than a push.

Every runtime call in this file has the same shape, `emit b (Sil.Apply (emit b (Sil.Func_ref
name) ty, args)) ty`; `rt.error_get` in the given code is a worked example of it, and
`rt.array_get` is one on this very type.

Reference: `solution/silgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase7-closures-stdlib/31-stdlib-array-string
```

Six files, and the two given ones are worth reading before you write anything.

- **`tests/silgen-reads.t`** and **`tests/sema-arrays.t`** are green from the start: everything
  you can do to an array without mutating it (literal, `count`, subscript, `for`-`in`, String,
  the multi-line literal, the out-of-bounds trap) and every type rule, including the three
  places we are smaller than Swift. Between them they define what your two mutators may assume.
- **`tests/silgen-append.t`** is `TODO(31a)`, and **`tests/silgen-subscript-set.t`** is
  `TODO(31b)`. They are independent — either can be filled first. Each shows the SIL shape
  (`make_unique` between the load and the write) and then the behaviour that shape buys: the
  fork on a shared buffer, the *absence* of a fork on a unique one, and the store-back, which is
  the step whose omission produces a program that runs, prints plausible numbers, and is wrong.
- **`tests/oracle.t`** asks swiftc every run: 20 programs whose verdict must match `swiftc
  -typecheck`, then 20 compiled four ways with stdout and exit code byte-identical to `swiftc
  -Onone`. Five of those twenty exist only to print the length and first element of an array
  that something else wrote to — value semantics is a claim about what does NOT happen, and the
  only way to test it is to look at the array nobody touched.
- **`tests/test_arrays.ml`** counts what cram can only imply: one `retain` per share and none
  for a fresh literal, one `make_unique` per mutation, and — walking the instruction stream in
  program order — that every `make_unique` result is the source of a later `store` into the slot
  it came from. That last one is the store-back bug, pinned structurally.

Reading the report: an untouched hole shows as `TODO … not started`; a hole in progress shows
`FAIL` with its passing cases still `OK`. `oracle.t` is `FAIL` rather than `TODO` from the
start, because its front-end half and its read-only programs pass before you write a line.

## 5. Benchmark it

The CoW payoff is measurable. Pass a large array to a function that only **reads** it (`for x in a
{ … }`): zero copies, because nothing mutates while shared. Now `var b = a; b.append(x)` inside the
loop: exactly one copy, on the first mutation. Compare against an eager-copy model (copy on every
assignment) — the difference is O(reads) copies avoided. swiftc's `Array` makes the same trade; the
microcost is one `refcount` load + compare per mutation, which the optimizer often hoists out of a
loop when it can prove uniqueness.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Element-generic buffers.** Make `[String]`/`[Bool]`/`[T]` work: keep the i64 buffer but
   `zext`/`ptrtoint` on push and `trunc`/`inttoptr` on get, driven by the element type. Lift the
   sema restriction. (This is the single most useful extension — it unlocks concept 32.)
2. **More `Array` API.** `remove(at:)`, `insert(_:at:)`, `first`/`last`, `+` (concatenate two
   arrays), `contains`. Each mutator reuses the make_unique dance; each reader is a new intrinsic.
3. **Reserve & uniqueness-hoisting.** Add `reserveCapacity(_:)` and, in `-O`, hoist a
   `make_unique` out of a loop when the array provably isn't aliased inside it — swiftc's
   "uniqueness propagation" optimization.
4. **Proper ARC for buffers.** Wire the buffer into concept 26's scope-release machinery: a
   `release` at scope exit that frees `data`+header at `refcount` 0. Verify no leaks with a
   counting allocator.
5. **A real `String`.** Move from C-string to a length-prefixed UTF-8 buffer; make `.count` count
   **graphemes** (or at least Unicode scalars) so non-ASCII matches `swiftc`.

## 7. Recap & what's next

An array is a **refcounted heap buffer** behind a pointer; **copy-on-write** — retain on share,
`make_unique` (copy iff `refcount > 1`) before a mutation, store the unique pointer **back** —
gives it **value semantics at reference speed**, exactly as `swiftc`'s `Array` does with
`isKnownUniquelyReferenced`. Reads share freely; only a write to a *shared* buffer pays a copy.
String is (for now) a C-string with concat and length. All of it lowers to **runtime intrinsics**
— no new SIL.

Next, **32-stdlib-collections** adds `Dictionary`/`Set`, the `Sequence`/`Collection` protocols,
and the higher-order trio **`map` / `filter` / `reduce`** — where concept-29 closures finally meet
concept-31 containers, **closing Milestone M7** (real-ish programs: closures over collections,
errors, value semantics, all matching `swiftc`).

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* 31a — a.append(x): the copy-on-write WRITE path *)
| Ast.Method_call (recv, m, args, _) when is_array_recv b recv && m = "append" ->
    let slot = array_slot b recv in
    let elt = (match vty b slot with Types.TArray el -> el | _ -> Types.TInt) in
    let xv = gen_expr_as b (snd (List.hd args)) elt in
    let p = emit b (Sil.Load slot) (vty b slot) in
    let uq =
      emit b (Sil.Apply (emit b (Sil.Func_ref "rt.array_make_unique") (vty b slot), [ p ])) (vty b slot)
    in
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (uq, slot)) Types.TVoid);
    let fr = emit b (Sil.Func_ref "rt.array_push") Types.TVoid in
    emit b (Sil.Apply (fr, [ uq; xv ])) Types.TVoid

(* 31b — a[i] = e: the same dance, ending in array_set *)
| Ast.Set_subscript { arr; index; value; _ } ->
    let slot = Hashtbl.find b.vars arr in
    let elt = (match vty b slot with Types.TArray el -> el | _ -> Types.TInt) in
    let iv = gen_expr b index in
    let xv = gen_expr_as b value elt in
    let p = emit b (Sil.Load slot) (vty b slot) in
    let uq =
      emit b (Sil.Apply (emit b (Sil.Func_ref "rt.array_make_unique") (vty b slot), [ p ])) (vty b slot)
    in
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (uq, slot)) Types.TVoid);
    let fr = emit b (Sil.Func_ref "rt.array_set") Types.TVoid in
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Apply (fr, [ uq; iv; xv ])) Types.TVoid)
```

The given `rt.array_make_unique` (in `irgen.ml`) is the CoW check itself:

```llvm
define private ptr @rt.array_make_unique(ptr %h) {
  %r = load i64, ptr %h            ; the refcount
  %shared = icmp sgt i64 %r, 1
  br i1 %shared, label %copy, label %keep
keep:
  ret ptr %h                       ; uniquely owned already — mutate in place
copy:
  %r1 = sub i64 %r, 1              ; drop our share of the original
  store i64 %r1, ptr %h
  ; … malloc a fresh header+data, copy `count` elements, refcount 1 …
  ret ptr %nh
}
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — element-generic buffers
Keep the i64 `data`, but convert at the SIL→LLVM boundary by the SIL element type: on `array_push`
`zext i1`/`ptrtoint ptr` the element to i64; on `array_get` `trunc`/`inttoptr` back. The runtime is
unchanged (still an i64 store); only the `Apply` lowering for `rt.array_*` grows a per-element-type
cast, and the sema restriction (`check_array_elt`) is dropped. Now `[String]` stores pointers and
`for s in names` works — which is precisely what concept 32's `map`/`filter` need.

### 2 — more Array API
Each *reader* (`first`, `contains`) is a new `rt.array_*` intrinsic + a sema rule. Each *mutator*
(`remove`, `insert`) reuses `array_slot` + the make_unique dance, differing only in the final
runtime call (which shifts elements). `a + b` (array concat) is a reader of both plus a fresh
buffer — no mutation, no make_unique.

### 3 — reserve & uniqueness hoisting
`reserveCapacity(n)` is make_unique then a runtime grow-to-`n`. The optimization: in a loop whose
body mutates `a` but where `a` is provably not aliased across iterations (no `var b = a` reaches
the loop), the `make_unique` is loop-invariant — hoist it to the preheader so the refcount check
runs once, not per iteration. This is LICM (a concept-18-adjacent pass) gated on an aliasing fact.

### 4 — proper ARC for buffers
Treat the buffer like a concept-26 managed value: `register_local` the slot, and at scope exit emit
`rt.array_release(p)` which decrements `refcount` and, at 0, frees `data` then the header. The
retain on `var b = a` (already emitted) now balances against these releases; a counting allocator
should report zero leaked blocks.

### 5 — a real String
Replace the C-string with `{ i64 count; i64 capacity; ptr utf8 }` (itself CoW, reusing this
concept's machinery). `.count` walks the UTF-8 grapheme boundaries (or, as a first step, counts
Unicode scalars). Now `"é".count == 1` and emoji count as one — matching `swiftc`'s
grapheme-cluster semantics instead of raw bytes.
```
